name: Thiel-Behnke corneal dystrophy
aliases: corneal dystrophy of Bowman layer type 2

reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / corneal dystrophy literature
clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant Bowman layer dystrophy, generally associated with the TGFBI gene
Produces a characteristic honeycomb pattern of subepithelial opacities
Presents in childhood or adolescence with recurrent corneal erosions
It runs a more slowly progressive and generally milder course than Reis-Bucklers dystrophy
Distinguishing it from Reis-Bucklers can require correlation of clinical, imaging, histological and genetic findings
Recurrent erosions are managed conservatively, with superficial ablation for visually significant opacity
reference.pathophysiology: Thiel-Behnke corneal dystrophy is a Bowman layer dystrophy, in most families linked to mutations in the TGFBI gene (distinct in phenotype from Reis-Bucklers). Abnormal protein deposition disrupts the Bowman layer, producing a honeycomb pattern of subepithelial opacities and impairing epithelial adhesion, which leads to recurrent corneal erosions from childhood. Opacification progresses slowly, gradually affecting vision, and, as with other anterior TGFBI dystrophies, the abnormality can recur after superficial treatment or grafting.
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination of the honeycomb subepithelial opacities
TGFBI genetic testing to confirm and distinguish from Reis-Bucklers
Assessment of erosion frequency and visual impact
Family history and examination of relatives
reference.prognosis: The course is slowly progressive and milder than Reis-Bucklers; vision is often preserved for longer, and superficial ablation can help, though recurrence is possible.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish it from Reis-Bucklers, which affects prognosis and surgical planning
Choosing penetrating keratoplasty when a superficial approach suffices
management: Manage recurrent corneal erosions conservatively with ocular lubricants, hypertonic saline, bandage contact lenses and prophylactic topical antibiotics during epithelial breakdown
Treat visually significant subepithelial opacity with superficial ablation — phototherapeutic keratectomy or superficial keratectomy
Reserve lamellar keratoplasty for advanced opacification not amenable to superficial treatment
Counsel that the dystrophy can recur in the treated cornea or graft, so plan for possible repeat procedures
Monitor visual acuity and erosion frequency at the slit lamp with anterior-segment imaging
Offer genetic counselling and examination of relatives, as this is an autosomal dominant TGFBI-associated dystrophy
